title: Batch vs Stream Processing
subtitle: Watch one shop's click events get turned into hourly revenue two ways, and see what each way costs you.
learn: How a MapReduce-style batch job splits, shuffles and reduces a big dataset
How a stream processor keeps running state and emits results continuously
What tumbling, sliding and session windows are and when to use each
Why late events happen and how watermarks decide when a window closes
How lambda and kappa architectures trade complexity for freshness and simplicity

steps.title: Same events, two ways to answer
steps.body: A shop's site and apps send about 5,000 events per second (clicks, carts, orders). That is roughly 430 million a day, or about 215 GB at 500 bytes each. The business wants revenue per hour on a dashboard. There are two ways to get it. You can let data pile up and crunch it in big jobs (batch). Or you can process each event the moment it arrives (stream). Either way, events first land in a durable event log.
steps.idea: Batch processes a finished pile of data. Stream processes data that never finishes.
steps.caption: Events flow from the sources into a durable log.

steps.title: Batch: collect, then compute
steps.body: Batch works on a bounded dataset: a fixed set of files with a known start and end. In the animation the log is copied into a data lake (cheap storage for raw files) as hourly files. Nothing is computed yet; the data just piles up. Because the input is complete and never changes, a failed job can simply be rerun on the same files and give the same answer.
steps.idea: A bounded input is finished and repeatable, so reruns are safe and simple.
steps.caption: Events are archived as hourly files.

steps.title: MapReduce: split, shuffle, reduce
steps.body: When an hour closes, the batch job reads that hour's files: about 9 GB (5,000 x 3,600 x 500 bytes). It cuts them into 128 MB splits, roughly 70 pieces. Map tasks run in parallel on the splits and emit (hour, amount) pairs. The shuffle sends all pairs with the same key to one reducer, and each reducer adds them up. Totals land in the serving store, the database the dashboard reads. Spark and similar engines use the same split, shuffle, aggregate idea. The job starts only after the hour ends, so the dashboard is over an hour behind (HUD: 4,200 s, about 70 min).
steps.idea: Batch scales by running many independent map tasks, then grouping by key. Its cost is waiting.
steps.caption: Parallel map and reduce tasks write hourly totals.

steps.title: Stream: compute as events arrive
steps.body: A stream processor reads the log continuously. Its input is unbounded: it never ends, so there is no final answer, only a running one. It keeps state in memory, such as a running revenue sum per hour. It updates that sum on every event and pushes fresh totals to the serving store. In the animation the dashboard asks for revenue and gets numbers about 2 seconds old, instead of over an hour old.
steps.idea: Streaming gives up the simplicity of finished input in return for results that are only seconds old.
steps.caption: Each event updates the running totals immediately.

steps.title: Windows: cutting an endless stream
steps.body: To get an hourly number from a never-ending stream, you cut it into windows. A tumbling window is fixed and does not overlap, like each clock hour. A sliding window overlaps: for example, the last hour recomputed every 5 minutes, so each event falls into 12 windows. A session window groups one user's activity and closes after a quiet gap, say 30 minutes.
steps.idea: Pick the window shape from the question: fixed buckets, a rolling view, or per-user activity.
steps.caption: The processor groups events into time windows.

steps.title: Late events and watermarks
steps.body: A phone loses signal and sends an order stamped 10:58 only at 11:03. Windows should use event time (when it happened), not processing time (when it arrived), or this order lands in the wrong hour. But the processor must decide when a window is finished. A watermark says 'I assume no event older than this is still coming'. It is often the newest event time minus a fixed wait, such as 2 minutes. This order is 5 minutes late, past that wait, so it counts as late. The processor can drop it, send it aside, or use it to correct the result. The 0.2% late rate is an assumed example.
steps.idea: A watermark is a guess about completeness. A shorter wait gives faster results but more late drops.
steps.caption: The order arrives after the 10:00-11:00 window has closed.

steps.title: Lambda: run both side by side
steps.body: Early stream engines gave approximate results and could lose data. So teams ran two paths over the same events. A speed layer (stream) gives quick but rough numbers. A batch layer recomputes accurate numbers later and overwrites them. The serving store merges the two. This works, but you write, test and debug the same business logic twice, in two systems, and the results must agree.
steps.idea: Lambda buys speed plus accuracy, at the price of two codebases that must match.
steps.caption: Batch and stream both write into one serving store.

steps.title: Kappa: one stream, replay for fixes
steps.body: Modern stream engines handle state, checkpoints and event time well, so kappa drops the batch path. The log is the source of truth and keeps data for days or months. To fix a bug or change logic, deploy the new version and replay the log from the start (offset 0) into a new output table. Then switch readers to it. A batch is just a stream that happens to end. The catch is retention: replay only works if the log still holds the history.
steps.idea: Kappa keeps one codebase by treating reprocessing as a replay of the log.
steps.caption: New code replays the log from offset 0.

steps.title: The stream job crashes
steps.body: The processor dies at 11:20 and loses 20 minutes of running totals held in memory. A batch task would simply rerun. A stream job instead takes periodic checkpoints: a snapshot of its state plus the log position (offset) it had reached, say every minute. On restart it reloads the last checkpoint and re-reads from that offset. We assume restart and catch-up take about 70 s, so the result lag spikes to 70 s. Some events are processed twice, so output writes must be idempotent (safe to repeat) or transactional, or totals would double count.
steps.idea: Checkpoint plus replay recovers a stream job. Idempotent output keeps the replay from double counting.
steps.caption: The job restores a checkpoint and re-reads the log.

steps.title: Choosing between them
steps.body: Use batch when hours of delay are fine and you need cheap, repeatable crunching of huge history, such as nightly reports or model training. Use stream when decisions need seconds, such as fraud checks or live dashboards. Streams need windows, event time and watermarks to cope with endless, out-of-order input. As a rule of thumb, prefer one codebase over lambda when your engine can replay the log or run the same code in batch mode.
steps.idea: Choose by how stale an answer you can accept, and pay for extra machinery only if you need it.
steps.caption: Batch is simple and hours old; stream is seconds old and needs more care.

quiz.q: An order happened at 10:58 on a phone with no signal and reached the stream processor at 11:03. Why should hourly windows use event time here?
options: Event time is always faster to compute
It removes the need for a log
The order belongs to the 10:00-11:00 hour, and arrival time would put it in the wrong one
Processing time cannot be used with windows
quiz.why: Event time records when something actually happened, so results stay correct despite delays. Processing time would count the order in 11:00-12:00 and change results whenever the pipeline is slow.

quiz.q: What is the main ongoing cost of a lambda architecture?
options: The log cannot store more than a day of data
The same business logic must be written and kept consistent in a batch system and a stream system
Batch jobs cannot read from the data lake
Serving stores cannot accept two writers
quiz.why: Lambda runs two code paths over the same events. Any logic change must be made twice, and the two paths can disagree, which is the main reason teams move to kappa.

quiz.q: Which workload fits batch processing best?
options: Recomputing a product-recommendation model over three years of purchase history each night
Blocking a stolen card within one second of a purchase
A live dashboard of orders in the last minute
Alerting when a sensor reads above a threshold
quiz.why: Large, bounded history with no need for second-level freshness is where batch is cheapest and simplest. The other three need results in seconds.

quiz.q: You find a bug in a kappa pipeline's revenue logic from last week. What is the sound fix?
options: Patch the running job and accept that last week's numbers stay wrong
Delete the log and wait for new events
Convert the pipeline to lambda immediately
Deploy the fixed job, replay the log from the needed offset into a new output, then switch readers to it
quiz.why: Kappa treats reprocessing as replay. This works only if the log's retention still covers the affected period, so retention is a design decision.

cheatsheet.def: Bounded data has a known end (a day's files), so batch can finish. Unbounded data never ends (live events), so stream jobs run forever.
Map tasks process input splits in parallel and emit key/value pairs; the shuffle groups equal keys; reduce tasks combine each group's values.
Fixed-size, non-overlapping buckets, such as each clock hour. Every event belongs to exactly one window.
Fixed size but advancing in smaller steps (1 hour every 5 minutes). Windows overlap, so each event counts in several.
Groups one key's events until a gap of inactivity (for example 30 minutes). Length varies per user.
Event time is when it happened; processing time is when the system sees it. Use event time for correct results under delays.
A moving estimate that no earlier events are still coming, often newest event time minus a fixed delay. It closes windows; later events are dropped or handled separately.
Lambda runs batch and stream paths and merges them. Kappa uses only a stream over a replayable log and reprocesses by replaying.
